The Bahá'í writings picture justice as the very foundation of human society. Shoghi Effendi describes it in [*God Passes By*](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) as ["the light of men"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) and the guardian upon which ["the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) depend, sustained by reward and punishment as its two pillars. 

At a personal level, Bahá’u’lláh defines its practical measure simply: ["Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ils_portals-to-freedom#p538), as noted in [*Portals to Freedom*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ils_portals-to-freedom#p538). Earl Redman's [*Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) likewise reminds us of the call in the Hidden Words that ["Justice is to be loved above all"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116). 

It is striking to see how deeply personal ethics and global order are bound together here. Does the connection between choosing for others what we choose for ourselves and the wider organization of the world feel natural to you, or is there a step between them you find yourself questioning?

Dear friend,

It is a joy to look into this with you. When we ask about justice in the Bahá'í writings, we find it described not merely as a legal rule or a social policy, but as a living, radiant force at the very center of human life. 

Shoghi Effendi writes in [God Passes By](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) that God extols justice 

> ["as the light of men and their guardian, as the revealer of the secrets of the world of being, and the standard-bearer of love and bounty"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*.

He affirms that upon justice must depend ["the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*, and he characterizes its two pillars—["reward and punishment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*—as the sources of life to the human race. 

There is also a profound inward and moral shape to this justice. In [Portals to Freedom](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ives_portals-to-freedom#p538), Howard Colby Ives points us to a definition given by Bahá’u’lláh: 

> ["Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ives_portals-to-freedom#p538) — *Portals to Freedom*.

This turns our gaze away from our own immediate personal reactions and asks us to measure our sense of fairness by how we treat our neighbor. In a similar spirit, Earl Redman records in [Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) that ['Justice is to be loved above all'](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) — *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*, spoken as a fundamental standard for both East and West.

Yet the writings also ground justice in divine law and order. J. Ruh-Angiz Bolles notes a passage from *Gleanings* where it says, 

> ["Know verily that the essence of Justice and the source thereof are both embodied in the ordinances prescribed by Him..."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/j-ruh-angiz-bolles_shoghi

You are pointing to something very real: human history is full of powerful people using the language of religion to justify their own rule. 

Might there not be another way to see it, though—where justice comes from a standard above any earthly power? In the Islamic tradition, the ultimate standard belongs not to rulers, but to the Divine, asking, ["Is not God a most just of judges?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_3792) — *The Qur’ân (Palmer)*. Similarly, in the Gathas, Zoroaster speaks of the bounteous spirit who chose ["the (Divine) Righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster?paraId=para_50) — *The Gathas*, placing the source of right actions far outside human politics. 

When texts point to a standard that exists independently of rulers, they offer a way to judge the powerful rather than just echoing them. How do you see the difference between justice defined by a king and justice defined by a higher law?

You see how laws and police step in when communities fray, and it is entirely natural to look at outward enforcement and think that is what holds society together. 

Might there not be another way to see it, though? Shoghi Effendi writes that ["Religion... is the greatest of all means for the establishment of order in the world"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_467) — *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*. From this view, outward laws are more like scaffolding, while what shapes the heart and brings real peace comes from deeper sources. 

Even in government, Confucius suggests that true order relies on moral force rather than punishment alone, saying the ruler's virtue acts ["as the wind, and that of inferior men as grass"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_514) — *The Analects*. 

And Lao-tzu observes that ["the more display there is of legislation, the more thieves and robbers there are"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu?paraId=para_279) — *Tao Te Ching*. 

It makes you wonder whether outward rules can ever create order on their own, or if they only respond after the inner foundation has already weakened. What do you think?

That view comes from a sincere desire to protect people from harm. But when governments rely on ["penal laws and in providing for ways and means of punishment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) — building prisons and chains—‘Abdu'l-Bahá suggests that ["in reality this only brings about the degradation of morals and the subversion of character"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952). 

Might there be another way to see it? Instead of forcing outward obedience through fear, the focus might be on education and inner growth. As ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains, the body politic should ["strive night and day, bending every effort to ensure that souls are properly educated"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) so that people freely ["acquire praiseworthy virtues and laudable manners"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952). Confucius similarly points toward moral leadership over force, noting that good men managing a country could eventually ["do away with capital punishments"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_553) entirely through the power of moral transformation.

It is a heavy thing to fall short of what we value. Confucius named this same weight as one of the things ["which weigh heavily upon my mind"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) — ["inability to walk according to knowledge received as to what is right and just"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247), alongside ["failure to improve in the virtues"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) — *The Analects*. 

Even when plans dissolve and efforts break down, as Mountfort Mills wrote when ["every time I try a plan of late the heavens – I hope it’s the heavens – open and it is no more"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mountfort-mills_two-letters-about-baghdad-property-case-to-horace-holley#p5), the turning back toward what is true is its own part of the path *Two letters about Baghdad property case to Horace Holley*.

You see something real: both traditions teach that supreme reality enters human history repeatedly. Bahá’u'lláh writes that ["Manifestations that are essentially one and the same"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) speak through different stations, while the Hindu texts describe divine figures as ["portions of the same Supreme Being"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-6_vyasa?paraId=fn_57). 

Yet there is a difference beneath the surface. Bahá'í Manifestations are distinct prophetic messengers sent in progressive ages to guide humanity, whereas Hindu avatars (such as Krishna or Rama) are descents of the Supreme Being into the material world to restore cosmic order, rooted in a cyclical cosmos. 

It is a wonder to trace how different traditions imagine the divine touching the earth. Which of these two views stirs your curiosity more?

Bahá’ís do not see all religions as exactly the same in every respect. Shoghi Effendi writes that the faith has assimilated ["varied races, nationalities, creeds and classes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_498) — which suggests that different creeds and traditions retain their distinct identities even as they find unity within the Bahá’í cause. 

While the passages provided here do not outline the specific Bahá’í view on the unity of religions, other traditions speak of a shared source or equal respect among prophets, such as the instruction in the Qur'an to ["make no difference between one and another of them"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_168) among the messengers sent from God (*The Holy Qur-an*). 

I read this as a distinction between recognizing a single divine origin for all authentic faiths and erasing their historical and theological differences. Might there be more to discover in how these diverse paths are understood to harmonize?

It is very easy to come to that view, since much of what is widely known about the Bahá'í teachings on this subject comes through the talks and writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá rather than the writings of Bahá'u'lláh Himself. 

Might there not be another way to see it, though? David Hofman writes that ["among the humanitarian principles which are explicit in His teaching"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) — referring to Bahá'u'lláh — is ["the equality of the sexes"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) *George Townshend, Hand of the Cause of God*. Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab similarly records 'Abdu'l-Bahá describing how ["in the revelation of Bahá’u’lláh, men and women stand shoulder to shoulder"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) and that ["the world of women will become all-refulgent and all-glorious. For His Holiness Bahá’u’lláh hath willed it so"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) *'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt*. 

I'll leave that with you to ponder alongside what you've read.

It is a wonderful thing to be touched by that vision. There is something lovely about how Gladys Weeden felt when she realized ["we are a world family dedicated to the unity of mankind"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) — *Gladys Weeden Pilgrim Notes*, noting simply that ["in the word “unity” the “you” comes before the “I.”"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) 

If you enjoy how different traditions look at our beginnings together, the Quran records that ["Mankind was but one nation"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1579) — *The Holy Qur-an (Yusuf Ali)* before differences arose. It is a quiet thought to carry with you.

You are right to connect the two names, as they belong to the same tradition and are closely linked. But they are distinct books. 

The *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* is described as [“the most signal act of His ministry”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) and serves as the principal repository of law, while the earlier *Kitáb-i-Íqán* is mentioned as the work where the Aqdas was [“Alluded to”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) beforehand. 

Shoghi Effendi records the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* as the ["Most Holy Book"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) whose laws are meant to guide the community for a thousand years.

I am so sorry for the loss of your father. 

When a soul departs, the Hindu texts speak of different paths according to its inner state at death: ["when a soul departeth, fixed In Soothfastness, it goeth to the place — Perfect and pure — of those that know all Truth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) — *The Bhagavad-Gita*, while a soul departing in ignorance ["is born anew in some unlighted womb"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) — *The Bhagavad-Gita*. In Buddhist texts, disciples also asked after those who had passed away to learn ["What are his movements after death?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1?paraId=para_362) — *Sutra Collection*.

It is a natural question, and one asked in many traditions—even in the book of Job, where people ask, ["What will we gain by offering prayer?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-book-of-job) *The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition*. 

When Ethel Stephana Stevens asked a similar question in *Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*, wondering why prayer is necessary "since presumably God knows the wishes of all hearts," she was told that prayer remains advocated. 

Might prayer be less about informing God and more about our own inner growth? As recorded in the Bahá'í accounts, [*Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35), "Every man is his own priest, is responsible for his own soul growth." Perhaps prayer is the deliberate turning of the heart that allows that growth to happen, independent of whether God already knows our needs.

It is completely understandable to feel hesitant about that claim, especially coming from a different tradition. 

Might there not be another way to see it, though? In the pilgrim records of *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*, it is noted that the figures of the Bahá'í faith ["praised and sanctified all the Divine Holy Manifestations, and offered His Holiness Christ such a praise, beyond the description and imagination"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. The text adds that Bahá'u'lláh even ["wrote many commentaries on the Gospel, bringing to light its inner significances"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. 

I leave it with you to see how those writings strike you.

I must be completely honest with you: the texts I have available right now don't actually mention Jesus or contain anything about him. 

The passages before me touch on alms and orphans in [*The Qur’ân*](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_146), the history of the early community in [*Ṣaḥíḥ al-Bukhárí*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-al-bukhari?paraId=para_13153) and [*Sahih Muslim*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-muslim-book-7_muslim-ibn-al-hajjaj?paraId=para_193), prophecy and miracles in Ibn Rushd's [*The Philosophy and Theology*](https://oceanlibrary.com/philosophy-and-thorology_ibn-rushd?paraId=para_141), Adam's prayer in [*Hayat Al-Qulub Vol.1*](https://oceanlibrary.com/hayat-al-qulub-vol-1_muhammad-majlisi?paraId=para_425), and commentary styles in Todd Lawson's study of the Báb's work. 

Because I rely solely on the evidence directly in front of me, I can't answer your question about Jesus from these sources. But I wonder — would you like to explore what these texts say about how prophets relate to miracles, or perhaps look elsewhere for what the Qur'án teaches?

I can't find anything about how Buddhism describes compassion in the texts I can search. 

The available passages touch on other topics, such as the formula for dependent co-arising, the virtue of monks, the discipline of the senses, and the nature of karma without an ego-entity in *The Gospel of Buddha* (https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/35895) — *The Gospel of Buddha*, but they do not address compassion directly. 

If you would like to explore what these texts say about virtue, karma, or the discipline of the senses, I would be very glad to look into those with you.

It is a very real doubt, especially when we look at how much the material world seems to explain on its own. 

Might there not be another way to see it, where investigation and faith speak to the same reality? In the Bahá'í writings, Doris McKay reflects on how ["Science and religion will enhance and prove each other"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) — *Memories of Bahá’ís*, asking, ["How can one truth contradict another truth?"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) Similarly, the commentary on the *Sutra Collection (HIJK)* suggests that a scientific world can accept teachings like the Kalama Sutta because there is ["not the least contradiction between the principles of science"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) and disciplined inquiry, since ["True scientists emphasize experimental verification"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) rather than mere opinion. 

Many scientists have felt that exploring the laws of nature uncovers a deeper order rather than replacing it.

I couldn't find anything on quantum computing in the texts I can search. 

The sources I can reach do not mention computers or modern processors. They do, however, speak of a broader current of knowledge and invention. Adib Taherzadeh writes in [_The Revelation of Bahá’u’lláh vol. 3_](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/adib-taherzadeh_the-revelation-of-bahaullah-vol-3#p1935) that Bahá’u’lláh affirmed that He would ["soon raise up scientists of great calibre who will bring about such marvellous technological achievements"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/adib-taherzadeh_the-revelation-of-bahaullah-vol-3#p1935) beyond present imagination. 

There is also a wonderful image in Shoghi Effendi's [_The Advent of Divine Justice_](https://oceanlibrary.com/advent-of-divine-justice_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_99) of a ["God-born Force... which, according to Bahá’u’lláh, has through its 'vibrating influence,' 'upset the equilibrium of the world and revolutionized its ordered life'"](https://oceanlibrary.com/advent-of-divine-justice_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_99).
